title: Thermal Suppression of Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions in Finite-Dimensional Systems A Quasi-Hermitian Framework
authors: Jia-Chen Tang, Xu-Yang Hou, Ming-Zhang Wang, Hao Guo
abstract: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in finite-dimensional systems prepared in thermal equilibrium states and subjected to a sudden quench. A mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude is constructed from first principles within a metric-stationary pseudo-Hermitian framework, providing a self-contained derivation of the finite-temperature quench dynamics. Applying this framework to an $N$-level model consisting of a two-level sector coupled to $N-2$ spectator states, we find that temperature controls the DQPTs through the redistribution of thermal weights among the eigenstates. This mechanism leads to a dimensionality-dependent threshold temperature that becomes finite when the Hilbert-space dimension reaches five, above which the Loschmidt amplitude loses all real zeros and the DQPTs are fully suppressed. The thermal suppression mechanism suggests a general principle for controlling dynamical criticality through thermal occupation, while the quasi-Hermitian framework provides the self-consistent foundation for its rigorous derivation.
summary: The paper rigorously analyzes Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions (DQPTs) in finite systems quenched from thermal equilibrium using a pseudo-Hermitian framework. It demonstrates that temperature acts as a control parameter, leading to a universal threshold temperature above which the DQPTs are entirely suppressed for sufficiently large system dimensions ($N \ge 5$). This establishes a general principle for controlling quantum criticality via thermal occupation.
main_problem: The study investigates how thermal effects suppress Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions (DQPTs) when a finite-dimensional system is quenched from a thermal equilibrium state.
main_result: A dimensionality-dependent threshold temperature ($T_{th}$) exists for $N \ge 5$, above which the DQPTs are fully suppressed because the Loschmidt amplitude loses all real zeros. The quasi-Hermitian framework provides the rigorous foundation for this derivation.
method: The authors construct and analyze a mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude using a metric-stationary pseudo-Hermitian framework, generalizing pure-state dynamics to thermal ensembles via purification.
model_or_system: The model is an $N$-level system composed of a two-level sector coupled to $N-2$ spectator states. The analysis focuses on the quench dynamics governed by quasi-Hermitian Hamiltonians ($H^\dagger = \eta H \eta^{-1}$).
key_observables: Mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude $G(t)$, its zeros (indicating DQPTs), and the rate function $r(t, T)$ exhibiting cusps at critical times.
important_parameters: System dimension ($N$), temperature ($T$ or $ eta$), and the metric operator ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The primary analysis relies on the fixed-metric (metric-stationary) quench assumption ($\eta_i = \eta_f$), which simplifies the dynamics by ensuring equivalence with a Hermitian system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the motion of Fisher zeros in the complex time plane, showing coalescence at $T_{th}$ for finite $N$, and demonstrate how rate function cusps vanish above a critical temperature $T^*$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude within the quasi-Hermitian framework. It then applies this to an N-level model, deriving explicit forms for $G(t)$ and identifying the condition for DQPTs based on thermal weights. Finally, it analyzes the temperature dependence leading to the finite threshold temperature.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful tool—the mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude in quasi-Hermitian settings—to study non-equilibrium critical phenomena (DQPTs) under realistic thermal conditions, linking quantum criticality directly to statistical mechanics principles.

Figure 1 displays the DQPT critical curves in the (t, T ) plane for N = 3, 4, and 5. All curves are periodic with period 2π and emanate from t = π/2 (mod 2π) at T = 0. For N = 3 (red), the critical time drifts from π/2 toward 2π/3 as T →∞, while for N = 4 (green) it approaches π in the same limit; in both cases DQPTs persist at all ﬁnite temperatures. For N = 5 (blue), the curve forms a closed loop: starting from t = π/2 at T = 0, it rises to a maximum temperature Tth = 2/ ln 2 at t = π, then descends to t = 3π/2 at T = 0.
